correctness.rationale: The two-impulse concentration follows from first-order linear kinetics. On each side of the second onset, the derivative has at most one positive-to-negative zero. For delayed onset strictly after the isolated peak, the derivative jumps upward by exactly the relative second dose, so a second local maximum exists precisely if \(m>-g'(d)=Q(d)\); equality produces no second maximum. The derivative \(Q'(d)\) has a unique zero at \(2t_0\) and its peak is the stated closed expression. Coincident rate constants and every equality and endpoint boundary are covered by a direct limiting formula. Direct code execution passed 2,200 randomized derivative/corner checks plus deterministic threshold tests; these are ancillary, not a substitute for the proof.

value.rationale: The two-input response is a natural simplified model of two releases or doses. A weak second input exhibits nonmonotone visual resolvability as its timing changes: two strict maxima just after the isolated first peak, one in an intermediate window, and two at late delays. The full if-and-only-if phase diagram, precise amplitude ceiling, and equality cases address an actual model boundary and can guide interpretation of idealized concentration profiles. It is not asserted as a clinical prescribing result.
